title: Replace a word in many files at once, with a preview and backups
summary: Finds every file in a folder that contains an old text and replaces it with a new text. You see the matching lines first. Each changed file keeps its original as a .bak copy next to it, so you can undo the change.

steps.explain: Preview: list every line that contains the old text. -F treats the text literally, so dots and stars are not special here. Nothing is changed.
steps.expect: Lines such as: config/app.conf:3:host=oldhost. Each file with a match shows up here.

steps.explain: Replace the text in every file that contains it. Each changed file gets a .bak copy first. Files that are already .bak copies are skipped. The slash in the replacement must not be part of the old or new text.
steps.expect: No output. Each changed file now has a matching .bak file next to it.

placeholders.name: OLD
placeholders.description: Text to replace; no slash or regex symbols

placeholders.name: DIR
placeholders.description: Same folder as in the preview

steps.explain: Check that the old text is gone. No output means no match is left outside the .bak copies.
steps.cmd: grep -rqF --exclude='*.bak' "<OLD>" <DIR> && echo 'old text still present' || echo 'no old text left'

rollback.explain: Put back the originals: every .bak file is moved over the file it copied. Do this only if you have not started other edits in those files.

warnings: The replacement also changes binary files and any file whose name is not filtered; use --include='*.conf' to limit the search.
The replace step is meant to run once. A second run changes the files again, and the .bak copies from the first run are not changed because of the exclude option.
A slash in the old or new text ends the sed pattern early. Escape it as a backslash slash, or avoid it.
